subject: mathematics
title: Counting and naming numbers to 100
scenes: Count these five chalk pieces. Point to each one and say one, two, three, four, five.
Start at twenty four and count by twos: twenty four, twenty six, twenty eight, thirty, thirty two.
Count by tens: ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty.
The fourth child has three children standing ahead. Fourth describes a position.

subject: mathematics
title: Finding numbers on a hundred chart
scenes: Look for twenty seven on our hundred chart. Here is the number twenty seven.
One step left from twenty seven is twenty six. One step right is twenty eight.
One row above twenty seven is seventeen. One row below is thirty seven.
Find fifty two. A row up is forty two, ten less. A row down is sixty two, ten more.

subject: mathematics
title: Measuring by counting handspans and cups
scenes: Place a handspan carefully along the same length without gaps. This door is eight handspans wide.
Use the same small cup each time. Bucket A holds five cupfuls.
Bucket B holds seven cupfuls with the same cup.
Seven cups is more than five cups. Bucket B has greater capacity.

subject: mathematics
title: More, less and ordering numbers
scenes: Look at fifteen, nine and twenty. Which comes first when we order the numbers?
Increasing order is nine, fifteen, twenty.
Decreasing order is twenty, fifteen, nine.
Thirty four has three tens. Forty three has four tens. Thirty four is less than forty three.

subject: mathematics
title: Greater than, less than and equal to
scenes: Seventeen is less than twenty one. Write the less than sign between them.
Ninety is greater than eighty nine. The greater than sign opens towards ninety.
Both groups have six mangoes. Six equals six.
Remember these three comparison signs: greater than, less than and equal to.

subject: mathematics
title: Comparing numbers in everyday stories
scenes: Yaw has eight crayons. Abena has five crayons.
Eight minus five is three. Yaw has three more crayons than Abena.
On this number sequence, fifteen is between twelve and nineteen.
Nineteen is the largest of these three numbers.

subject: mathematics
title: Understanding addition and subtraction
scenes: Ama has six books and gets two more books. Join the groups.
Six plus two equals eight. We add when groups join together.
Kojo has twelve oranges and gives away five.
Twelve minus five equals seven. Seven oranges remain.

subject: mathematics
title: Understanding equal groups and missing numbers
scenes: Eight equals five plus three. Both sides have the same value.
Combine five objects and three objects. Together there are eight.
Ten minus what number gives seven?
Take away three from ten to leave seven. The missing number is three.

subject: mathematics
title: Addition and subtraction are connected
scenes: Three counters and five counters make eight.
We can write three plus five equals eight.
If we remove five from eight, three remain.
If we remove three from eight, five remain. These facts belong to one family.

subject: mathematics
title: Making stories from number sentences
scenes: Seven children are playing. Five friends arrive and join them.
Seven plus five equals twelve children altogether.
Fourteen bananas are in a bowl. Six are taken away.
Fourteen minus six equals eight bananas left in the bowl.

subject: mathematics
title: Friendly number facts and doubles
scenes: Seven and three are number partners. They fill ten spaces.
Seven plus three equals ten.
Double four means four added to four.
Double four is eight. Learn doubles to calculate quickly.

subject: mathematics
title: Smart ways to add and subtract within 20
scenes: Start with nine. Take one from four to complete ten.
Nine plus four becomes ten plus three.
Ten plus three is thirteen. So nine plus four is thirteen.
For subtraction, sixteen minus five is eleven.

subject: mathematics
title: One-step word problems
scenes: There are seven girls and six boys. How many children altogether?
We add the groups. Seven plus six equals thirteen children.
A farmer has eighteen eggs and sells nine eggs.
Subtract because some are sold. Eighteen minus nine equals nine eggs.

subject: mathematics
title: Finding one-half
scenes: Fold a rectangular paper into two equal parts.
Shade one of two equal parts of a circle. This is one half.
Put the two equal halves together. They make one whole.
If the parts are not equal, we cannot call each part one half.

subject: mathematics
title: Counting halves
scenes: This is one half piece.
Add another equal half piece. Two halves make one whole.
Now we have three half pieces, making one whole and one extra half.
Four half pieces can be paired to make two wholes.

subject: mathematics
title: Ghanaian coins and their values
scenes: Two twenty pesewa coins are worth forty pesewas.
Five twenty pesewa coins make one hundred pesewas.
Two fifty pesewa coins also make one hundred pesewas.
One hundred pesewas equal one Ghana cedi.

subject: mathematics
title: Repeating patterns around us
scenes: Circle, square, circle, square. What comes next?
The next shape is a circle because the unit repeats.
One, two, three, one, two, three. What comes next?
The next number is one. The unit has three numbers.

subject: mathematics
title: How we know a shape
scenes: This triangle has three straight sides.
Turn the triangle. It remains a triangle because it still has three straight sides.
A square is flat, like a drawing on paper.
A cube is solid and takes up space. Its flat faces are squares.

subject: mathematics
title: Solid shapes in the home and school
scenes: A football is like a sphere. A can is like a cylinder.

A cone has a pointed tip. A triangular prism has triangular ends.
Look for these solid shapes at home and school.

subject: mathematics
title: Flat shapes and their properties
scenes: Count the six straight sides of the hexagon.
A rectangle has four sides and four right angle corners.
A circle has a curved edge. A triangle has three sides. A square has four equal sides.
A rhombus has four equal sides. Its corners do not need to be right angles.

subject: mathematics
title: Position and direction words

We can move left, right, up and down.

subject: mathematics

Eight cups is greater than four cups. The bucket has more capacity.

subject: mathematics

subject: english

The answer is: mar-ket. Break longer words into syllables, then blend them.

subject: english
title: Word Parts and Rhyming Endings

subject: english
title: Picture a Story and Read Smoothly

subject: english
title: 120 Reading Words and Self-Correction

subject: english
title: Draw Labels and Write How You Feel

The answer is: We grow green vegetables.. All sentences in a paragraph should develop one idea.

subject: english
title: Write About Experiences and Feelings

The answer is: I feel happy.. A sentence can name a person’s feelings.

subject: english
title: Describing People, Events and Dates
scenes: A useful oral description includes specific details: who, what, where, when and how.
What makes a spoken description useful? Answer: Specific details about what happened and where.
Describe a recent school event with its date, place and two important details.
Discuss why: Details help the listener imagine events.

subject: english
title: Attentive Listening and Viewing
scenes: Good listeners attend to the complete message and take brief notes before answering.
“Ama sorted paper and plastic into separate bins.” What is the main idea? Answer: Ama separated waste for recycling.
Listen to a partner's one-minute announcement and record the place, time and purpose.
Discuss why: The central action is sorting waste.

subject: english
title: Conversations and Turn-Taking
scenes: Good conversations balance speaking and listening, ask relevant questions and respect other opinions.
Someone is speaking in a group. What is a respectful response? Answer: Listen until the speaker finishes.
Discuss how to keep the school compound clean; invite a partner's different view.
Discuss why: Turn-taking lets all ideas be heard.

subject: english
title: Using Story Clues and Life Experience — Part 1
scenes: Connect story events with prior knowledge; identify the main idea, compare events and infer a moral.
Why is a story's setting useful? Answer: It tells where or when events happen.
Read a short story aloud and explain which event is most important and why.
Discuss why: Setting places events in a context.

subject: english
title: Using Story Clues and Life Experience — Part 2
scenes: Connect story events with prior knowledge; identify the main idea, compare events and infer a moral.
Kojo lost a book, searched his bag, then found it in class. What happened first? Answer: Kojo lost the book.
Read a short story aloud and explain which event is most important and why.
Discuss why: The loss starts the sequence.

subject: english
title: Pronunciation and Intonation
scenes: Meaning changes with clear pronunciation and appropriate voice pitch in statements and questions.
Which action improves reading fluency? Answer: Read familiar passages aloud with expression.
Read the same sentence as a question and as a statement, then compare the tone.
Discuss why: Practice supports pace and expression.

subject: english
title: Question Tags in Conversation
scenes: A positive statement commonly takes a negative question tag; a negative statement takes a positive tag.
Complete: “She is here, blank ?” Answer: isn't she
Have a partner turn five statements into polite confirmation questions.
Discuss why: A positive 'is' statement takes 'isn't she?'.

subject: english
title: Giving Instructions and Polite Requests
scenes: Instructions use clear verbs in a useful order; polite requests say please or could you.
Which question seeks another person's view? Answer: What do you think about planting trees?
Explain how to plant a seed using three commands, then request help politely.
Discuss why: The first asks for an opinion.

subject: english
title: Voice, Gesture and Meaning
scenes: Spoken communication uses volume, pace, stress, facial expressions and gestures to support meaning.
A learner rushes and misses small words. What should improve? Answer: Slow to a manageable pace and check accuracy.
Describe how a friendly greeting differs from an angry warning.
Discuss why: Accurate pace supports comprehension.

subject: english
title: Clear and Fluent Speaking
scenes: Speak audibly at an appropriate pace, pause at punctuation and pronounce words clearly.
What is the purpose of a full stop during oral reading? Answer: Pause and mark the end of a sentence.
Record or present a short announcement with natural pauses and correct stress.
Discuss why: Pausing marks the sentence ending.

subject: english
title: Planning an Effective Speech — Part 1
scenes: A speech needs an audience, purpose, selected facts, clear introduction, ordered points and effective conclusion.
What helps a paragraph stay focused? Answer: One central idea with related details.
Present a one-minute speech about reading habits with an opening, two facts and a closing.
Discuss why: A focused paragraph has a clear topic.

subject: english
title: Planning an Effective Speech — Part 2
scenes: A speech needs an audience, purpose, selected facts, clear introduction, ordered points and effective conclusion.
Which sentence is a topic sentence? Answer: Our school garden needs regular care.
Present a one-minute speech about reading habits with an opening, two facts and a closing.
Discuss why: A topic sentence introduces the paragraph's main point.

subject: english
title: Letter Patterns and Consonant Digraphs
scenes: Consonant digraphs such as sh, ch and ck form familiar sounds; sounds help decode words.
Which word begins with the digraph sh? Answer: ship
Read and write five words containing sh, ch or ck; use two in sentences.
Discuss why: The letters sh represent a single consonant sound.

subject: english
title: Using Prefixes to Decode Words
scenes: Prefixes attach before a root word; re-, un- and dis- can change meaning.
What does re- usually suggest in “rewrite”? Answer: Write again
Build and explain three words with prefixes, such as retell and unhappy.
Discuss why: Re- commonly means again.

subject: english
title: Rhyming Endings and Digraphs
scenes: Word families share end sounds; digraphs can appear at the beginning or end of words.
Which word rhymes with sand? Answer: hand
Group words by a common rhyme, then write a sentence using a digraph word.
Discuss why: Sand and hand share their final sound.

subject: english
title: Diphthongs in Everyday Words
scenes: Diphthongs are vowel sounds that glide, as in day, time and boy.
Which word has the /oi/ sound? Answer: coin
Sort ten spoken words into day, time and boy sound groups.
Discuss why: Coin contains /oi/.

subject: english
title: Sound Blending and Spelling
scenes: Blend sounds in order to read a word; use letter-sound links to spell it.
Which pair uses the same digraph? Answer: shop and shell
Blend three new words aloud, then write and check their spelling.
Discuss why: Both shop and shell start with sh.

subject: english
title: Content Vocabulary and Compound Words
scenes: Words can name precise school topics; compound words combine meaningful word parts.
What is a compound word? Answer: Two smaller words joined into one.
Keep a vocabulary notebook and explain the two parts of three compounds.
Discuss why: Compound words combine meaningful parts.

subject: english
title: Building a Reading Vocabulary
scenes: Wide reading grows vocabulary; rereading and noting unfamiliar words helps retention.
Which word best describes someone who helps others? Answer: helpful
Read a short passage and record four new words with guessed meanings.
Discuss why: Helpful means ready to assist.

subject: english
title: Word Meaning from Context
scenes: Surrounding words, relationships and sentence clues help reveal unfamiliar word meanings.
“The path was narrow, so only one person could walk across.” Narrow means what? Answer: Not wide
Underline a clue in a sentence that helps you infer the meaning of a new word.
Discuss why: Only one person fits across the path.

subject: english
title: Affixes, Wordplay and Register
scenes: Adding affixes changes a word's meaning; choose language to suit audience and purpose.
What does dis- mean in “disagree”? Answer: Not agree
Change five root words using prefixes or suffixes and write an appropriate message.
Discuss why: Dis- can express opposition.

subject: english
title: Main Ideas and Close Reading
scenes: Read closely to identify the main idea and important supporting details; skim when looking for a gist.
“An old tree shaded the school playground.” Which detail shows a benefit? Answer: It shaded the playground.
Highlight one topic sentence and list three details that support it.
Discuss why: Shade is a benefit for learners.

subject: english
title: Reading Evidence and Personal Connections
scenes: An interpretation should point to text evidence; personal connections support but do not replace the text.
“Ama sorted paper and plastic into separate bins.” What is the main idea? Answer: Ama separated waste for recycling.
Explain a character's choice using one sentence from a story as evidence.
Discuss why: The central action is sorting waste.

subject: english
title: Meaning of Words in a Passage
scenes: Determine word meaning from how it is used, rather than selecting a dictionary sense at random.
“Ama was relieved when she found her missing key.” Relieved means what? Answer: No longer worried
Find two words with more than one meaning and explain the sense used in a passage.
Discuss why: Finding the key removes worry.

subject: english
title: Independent Silent Reading
scenes: Read silently for meaning, pause at confusing parts and check answers against the passage.
“The class planted seeds on Monday; shoots appeared Friday.” What happened last? Answer: Shoots appeared.
Read a short passage silently, then answer who, where, why and what-next questions.
Discuss why: The final event is growth on Friday.

subject: english
title: Reading Fluently and Checking Meaning
scenes: Fluent readers use accurate words, a suitable pace and natural expression while checking understanding.
What should a reader do after an unfamiliar word? Answer: Blend or decode it, then reread the sentence.
Read one paragraph aloud; repeat more smoothly, then explain its message.
Discuss why: Decoding and rereading restore meaning.

subject: english
title: Oral and Written Summaries
scenes: A good summary includes the central point and essential events without copying every detail.
What belongs in an effective summary? Answer: The main idea and essential points.
Give an oral summary, then write a three-sentence summary in your own words.
Discuss why: Summaries are concise and selective.

subject: english
title: Common, Proper, Collective and Abstract Nouns
scenes: Nouns name people, places, things, groups and ideas. Proper names begin with capitals.
Which word is a proper noun? Answer: Kumasi
Find and label one common, proper, collective and abstract noun in a story.
Discuss why: A specific place name is a proper noun.

subject: english
title: Articles, Quantifiers and Determiners — Part 1
scenes: Articles, demonstratives and quantifiers help identify which noun or how much is meant.
Which article completes “ blank orange”? Answer: an
Write sentences using a, an, the, some, these and which correctly.
Discuss why: Use an before a vowel sound.

subject: english
title: Articles, Quantifiers and Determiners — Part 2
scenes: Articles, demonstratives and quantifiers help identify which noun or how much is meant.
Which article completes “ blank orange”? Answer: an
Write sentences using a, an, the, some, these and which correctly.
Discuss why: Use an before a vowel sound.

subject: english
title: Choosing the Right Pronoun
scenes: Pronouns replace nouns to avoid repetition and must agree with who or what they refer to.
Replace Ama in “Ama sings well.” Answer: She
Rewrite a paragraph with repeated names using clear pronouns.
Discuss why: She is a subject pronoun.

subject: english
title: Comparative and Superlative Adjectives
scenes: Use comparative forms to compare two things and superlatives to compare three or more.
Choose the comparative of tall. Answer: taller
Compare two trees and then describe the tallest of three trees.
Discuss why: Taller compares two things.

subject: english
title: Verb Types and Subject–Verb Agreement — Part 1
scenes: Verbs show actions or states. Singular and plural subjects need matching verb forms.
Complete “Esi blank to school each day.” Answer: walks
Underline each subject and correct its verb in six sentences.
Discuss why: A singular third-person subject takes walks in the simple present.

subject: english
title: Verb Types and Subject–Verb Agreement — Part 2
scenes: Verbs show actions or states. Singular and plural subjects need matching verb forms.
Which is a verb in “Kofi carried a basket”? Answer: carried
Underline each subject and correct its verb in six sentences.
Discuss why: Carried shows an action.

subject: english
title: Adverbs of Time and Place
scenes: Adverbs of time tell when; adverbs of place tell where an action happens.
Which word tells when an action happened? Answer: yesterday
Describe classroom actions using yesterday, soon, here and outside.
Discuss why: Yesterday is an adverb of time.

subject: english
title: Understanding Everyday Idioms
scenes: An idiom carries a meaning beyond the literal words, so context matters.
What does “lend a hand” usually mean? Answer: Help someone
Discuss three everyday idioms and explain their meanings in your own words.
Discuss why: The idiom means help.

subject: english
title: Connecting Ideas with Conjunctions
scenes: Conjunctions such as and, but, or and nor connect ideas and show their relationship.
Complete “Ama blank Kofi read together.” Answer: and
Join sentence pairs using two different conjunctions and discuss the change in meaning.
Discuss why: And connects two people doing an activity.

subject: english
title: Modals for Rules, Ability and Advice
scenes: Can, may, must, should and might signal ability, permission, duty, advice and possibility.
Which modal expresses ability? Answer: can
Write school rules using must and helpful suggestions using should.
Discuss why: Can commonly expresses ability.

subject: english
title: Prepositions for Place, Time and Purpose
scenes: Prepositions show relationships involving place, time, direction, purpose and comparison.
Complete “The ball is blank the table.” Answer: under
Describe locations and schedules using beside, between, at, for and than.
Discuss why: Under shows position.

subject: english
title: Neat Handwriting and Complete Sentences
scenes: A complete sentence needs an understandable subject and predicate; writing should be clear and consistent.
What is the subject of “The pupils planted maize”? Answer: The pupils
Copy a paragraph neatly and mark each sentence's subject and predicate.
Discuss why: The subject names who performed the action.

subject: english
title: Choosing a Purpose and Organising Ideas
scenes: Writers choose a format for their audience and build a main idea with supporting details.
Which sentence is a topic sentence? Answer: Our school garden needs regular care.
Plan a paragraph about water conservation for a school noticeboard.
Discuss why: A topic sentence introduces the paragraph's main point.

subject: english
title: Selecting and Narrowing a Topic
scenes: A focused topic can be explained with specific facts, rather than many unrelated ideas.
Why make a plan before writing? Answer: To organise ideas logically.
Choose one issue at school, brainstorm details and write a focused topic sentence.
Discuss why: Planning guides the draft.

subject: english
title: Writing a First Paragraph Draft
scenes: A first draft arranges a topic sentence and supporting points in a logical order.
Why make a plan before writing? Answer: To organise ideas logically.
Write a six-sentence paragraph draft about a healthy school lunch.
Discuss why: Planning guides the draft.

subject: english
title: Revising, Proofreading and Publishing
scenes: Revise ideas and order first; proofread spelling, grammar and punctuation before sharing.
Which step checks ideas and organisation? Answer: Revising
Exchange a paragraph with a partner and mark one revision and two corrections.
Discuss why: Revision improves meaning and structure.

subject: english
title: Narrating Real and Imagined Events
scenes: Narratives describe characters, a setting, a problem and events in time order.
Why is a story's setting useful? Answer: It tells where or when events happen.
Write a short account of a surprising school-day event with a clear ending.
Discuss why: Setting places events in a context.

subject: english
title: Creative Writing and Imagination
scenes: Creative writing uses original details, imagery and a meaningful sequence.
A poem has four lines. How many lines will you write? Answer: Four
Invent a four-line poem and a short story opening about a rainy market day.
Discuss why: A four-line poem contains four lines.

subject: english
title: Describing People and Places
scenes: Specific adjectives and sensory details help a reader picture a place or person.
When reporting a school event, which detail gives time? Answer: Friday morning at nine.
Describe a busy market using sight, sound and movement without repeating adjectives.
Discuss why: A stated time locates the event.

subject: english
title: Expressing an Opinion with Reasons
scenes: State your opinion clearly and support it with a reason and an example.
Which sentence states an opinion? Answer: Our school should have a reading corner.
Write three sentences about why reading time matters at school.
Discuss why: Should signals a view or proposal.

subject: english
title: Claims, Evidence and Persuasive Conclusions
scenes: A persuasive paragraph states a claim, adds reasons and ends with a conclusion.
Which transition introduces a reason? Answer: because
Write a paragraph arguing for a school reading corner using two reasons.
Discuss why: Because explains why.

subject: english
title: Writing Useful Information About Family
scenes: Informative writing uses clear factual details and suitable language for the reader.
Which sentence is a topic sentence? Answer: Our school garden needs regular care.
Write an accurate family description while respecting people's privacy.
Discuss why: A topic sentence introduces the paragraph's main point.

subject: english
title: Writing from a Picture Sequence
scenes: Picture stories need an order of events and connections between each picture.
A child returned extra change to a trader. Which value did the child show? Answer: Honesty
Draw three pictures showing a helpful action and write one sentence per picture.
Discuss why: Returning what is not yours is honest.

subject: english
title: Writing a Friendly Letter
scenes: A friendly letter includes an address or location, date, greeting, message and suitable closing.
What should open a friendly letter? Answer: A suitable greeting such as Dear Esi,
Write a letter to a friend describing a school activity and inviting a reply.
Discuss why: A greeting addresses the recipient.

subject: english
title: Using Commas Correctly
scenes: A comma separates items in a list and may separate an introductory phrase.
Which sentence separates three items correctly? Answer: We bought yam, rice and fish.
Edit six sentences using commas in lists and after opening phrases.
Discuss why: Commas can separate items in a list.

subject: english
title: Nouns in Written Sentences
scenes: Choose common, proper, collective and abstract nouns to make writing precise.
Which word is a collective noun? Answer: team
Highlight four different types of nouns in a paragraph and revise repeated wording.
Discuss why: Team names a group.

subject: english
title: Verb Tenses and Agreement in Writing
scenes: Match subjects and verbs; keep verb time consistent unless the meaning requires a change.
Which is a verb in “Kofi carried a basket”? Answer: carried
Edit a paragraph that shifts incorrectly between past and present tense.
Discuss why: Carried shows an action.

subject: english
title: Comparative Adjectives in Writing
scenes: Choose correct comparative and superlative forms, including irregular forms.
Choose the comparative of tall. Answer: taller
Compare three classroom objects in complete sentences.
Discuss why: Taller compares two things.

subject: english
title: Where and When: Adverbs in Writing
scenes: Adverbs such as yesterday and nearby describe the time or place of actions.
Which word tells when an action happened? Answer: yesterday
Use four different adverbs to make a travel account more precise.
Discuss why: Yesterday is an adverb of time.

subject: english
title: Meaningful Prepositions in Writing
scenes: Prepositions connect words to show relationships of position, direction, time, purpose and comparison.
Which preposition shows movement in “Walk blank the gate”? Answer: towards
Edit five sentences where prepositions are missing or used incorrectly.
Discuss why: Towards shows direction.

subject: english
title: Joining Sentences and Ideas
scenes: Join ideas with appropriate conjunctions so the relationship between them is clear.
Complete “Ama blank Kofi read together.” Answer: and
Combine three pairs of sentences with and, but, or or because.
Discuss why: And connects two people doing an activity.

subject: english
title: Subjects, Predicates and Sentences
scenes: A complete sentence says who or what it is about and what happens or is true.
What is the subject of “The pupils planted maize”? Answer: The pupils
Divide five sentences into subject and predicate and correct two fragments.
Discuss why: The subject names who performed the action.

subject: english
title: Spelling by Sounds and Checking Words
scenes: Invented spelling can help first drafts; check conventional spellings before publishing.
Choose the correctly spelt word. Answer: beautiful
Write difficult words as you hear them, then check with a word list or dictionary.
Discuss why: Beautiful has the correct letter order.

subject: english
title: Independent Reading and Book Summaries
scenes: Reading for pleasure develops vocabulary and knowledge. A two-paragraph book summary includes key events and a thoughtful response.
How should a learner write a summary? Answer: Use their own words where possible.
Choose an age-appropriate book; write two short summary paragraphs and recommend it to a friend.
Discuss why: Paraphrasing shows understanding.

subject: mathematics
title: Building place value & Reading large numbers
scenes: Learn to model number quantities, place value for multi-digit using graph sheets or multi-base materials up to 100,000 and read and write numbers in figures and in words up 100,000
How many complete groups of 1 are in 14,682? The answer is 14682. 14,682 divided by 1 has 14682 complete groups.
A school has 72,215 bottle tops. How many complete bundles of 10 can it make? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 7221. 72,215 divided by 10 gives 7221 full bundles.

subject: mathematics
title: The number chart & Comparing and ordering
scenes: Learn to identify numbers in different positions around a given number in a number chart and compare and order whole numbers up to 10,000 and represent comparisons using the symbols “ less than ”, “ equals ”, “ greater than ”
On a number chart with steps of 1,000, what is directly after 1,270? The answer is 2,270. Move forward one step of 1,000.
Kofi is on box 3,545 of a number chart counting by 10. What box comes next? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 3,555. Add 10.

subject: mathematics
title: Rounding numbers & Skip counting
scenes: Learn to round (off, up, down) whole numbers up to 10000 to the nearest, thousands, hundreds and tens and skip count forwards and backwards in 50s and 100s up to and from 10000
Round 3,116 up to the next multiple of 10. The answer is 3,120. Use groups of 10 and the instruction “round up to”.
A market records about 8,695 visitors. Estimate to the nearest 100. Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 8,700. Round 8,695 to the nearest 100.

subject: mathematics
title: Discover Roman numerals & Convert Roman numerals
scenes: Learn to develop an understanding of roman numeral system up xxx (i.e. 30) and count and convert hindu arabic numerals to roman numerals up to 30 and vice versa
Which Roman numeral represents 1? The answer is I. I equals 1, V equals 5 and X equals 10; IV equals 4, IX equals 9.
A scoreboard uses Roman numbers. Which symbol should appear for position 6? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is VI. Build Roman numerals using X, V and I.

subject: mathematics
title: Factors & Highest common factors
scenes: Learn to determine set of factors of a given numbers up to 50 and determine the highest common factor (hcf) of any two whole numbers between 1 and 50
27 objects are put into groups of 9. How many groups are made? The answer is 3. Factors make equal groups.
A gardener plants 18 seedlings in equal rows of 9. How many complete rows are needed? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 2. 18 divided by 9 equals 2.

subject: mathematics
title: Lowest common multiples & Factors and multiples
scenes: Learn to determine the lowest common multiple (lcm) of at least any two given numbers up to 100 and recognise the relationship between factors and multiples
Find the lowest common multiple (LCM) of 8 and 13. The answer is 104. 104 is the smallest positive multiple of both numbers.
A bell rings every 4 minutes and a drum every 5 minutes. Starting together, after how many minutes will they next sound together? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 20. Find LCM(4, 5) equals 20.

subject: mathematics
title: Square-number patterns & Square arrays
scenes: Learn to generate and analyse patterns in square numbers and represent square numbers using factors
Continue the square-number sequence: 289, 324, blank . The answer is 361. Square numbers are 1 times 1, 2 times 2, 3 times 3, .
A pattern uses square tiles: 1, 4, 9, 16, ... Which number represents a 12 by 12 square? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 144. 12 squared equals 144.

subject: mathematics
title: Negative numbers around us & Crossing zero on a number line
scenes: Learn to describe real life situations using positive and negative values and count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers through zero
The temperature is 4 degrees C. It becomes 2 degrees C colder. What is the new temperature? The answer is 2 degrees C. Colder means subtract 2.
A mountain village is at 9 degrees C. The reading changes by minus 3 degrees C. What temperature is recorded? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 6 degrees C. Add the signed change: 9 minus 3 equals 6.

subject: mathematics
title: Multiplication facts
scenes: Learn to recall multiplication facts through the tables up to 11 times 11
Calculate 4 times 10. The answer is 40. 4 groups of 10 give 40.
There are 4 trays with 4 oranges in each. How many oranges are there altogether? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 16. 4 times 4 equals 16.

subject: mathematics
title: Doubling as a strategy & Mental multiplication
scenes: Learn to apply mental mathematics strategies and number properties, such as skip counting from a known fact using doubling or halving using patterns in the 9s facts using repeated doubling or halving to determine answers for basic multiplication facts to 81 and related division facts and apply mental mathematics strategies for multiplication, such as annexing then adding zero halving and doubling using the distributive property
You know 4 times 3 equals 12. What is 8 times 3 by doubling? The answer is 24. Double 12 to get 24.
8 baskets hold 7 tomatoes each. Twice as many baskets are filled the same way. How many tomatoes are there? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 112. Double 8 times 7 equals 112.

subject: mathematics
title: Multiplying large numbers
scenes: Learn to multiply multi-digit numbers efficiently
Work out 195 times 9. The answer is 1755. Multiply ones, then tens and hundreds; total 1755.
There are 200 trays with 5 oranges in each. How many oranges are there altogether? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 1000. 200 times 5 equals 1000.

subject: mathematics
title: Division facts
scenes: Learn to determine basic division fact up to 81
Find 48 divided by 6. The answer is 8. Because 8 times 6 equals 48, 48 divided by 6 equals 8.
A teacher puts 36 mangoes into sets of 4. How many full sets can she make? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 9. 4 times 9 equals 36.

subject: mathematics
title: Dividing by one-digit numbers
scenes: Learn to divide 2-digit numbers by 1-digit number efficiently
Divide 36 divided by 4. The answer is 9. 4 times 9 equals 36.
A teacher puts 244 mangoes into sets of 4. How many full sets can she make? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 61. 4 times 61 equals 244.

subject: mathematics
title: Two-step word problems
scenes: Learn to solve multi-step word problems involving the four basic operations

A class collected 21 blue and 6 green bottle tops, then shared them into 4 equal groups. How many complete bottle tops per group? The answer is 6. 21 plus 6 equals 27; divide by 4 for 6 complete items (with 3 left over).
A class has 21 blue beads and 17 red beads. It makes 5 equal necklaces. How many whole items can each get? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 7. 21 plus 17 equals 38; 38 divided by 5 gives 7 each with 3 left.

subject: mathematics
title: Unit fractions on number lines & Equivalent fractions
scenes: Learn to partition the 0 to 1 number line into equal unit fractions and recognise and name equivalent fractions using pictorial representations and number line to determine the lowest common denominator (lcd)
A number line from 0 to 1 is divided into 6 equal parts. What fraction is at mark 4 after zero? The answer is 4/6. Each tick is one 6th, so mark 4 is 4/6.
A measuring strip is divided into 8 equal sections. 4 are coloured. What fraction is coloured? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 4/8. 4 parts out of 8.

subject: mathematics
title: Simplifying fractions & Improper fractions
scenes: Learn to find the simplest form of given fractions by dividing through by the highest common factor (i.e. by cancelling through by factors) and recognise fractions that are greater than one (i.e. improper fractions), draw and label such fractions with their symbols
Simplify 42/84 to lowest terms. The answer is 1/2. Divide by 7 and simplify any other common factor.
A shaded diagram shows 18 out of 21 equal squares. What is this fraction in lowest terms? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 6/7. Divide numerator and denominator by their common factor.

subject: mathematics
title: Comparing fractions & Everyday fractions
scenes: Learn to compare and order fractions with like denominators by using pictorial representations and finding equivalent fractions using the lowest common denominator (lcd) and provide examples of where fractions are used
Which fraction is greater: 2/4 or 3/4? The answer is 3/4. With equal denominators, the larger numerator gives the larger fraction.
Two ribbons are 2/8 m and 7/8 m long. Which is longer? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 7/8. With equal denominators compare numerators.

subject: mathematics
title: Tenths and hundredths & Rounding decimals
scenes: Learn to describe and represent decimals (tenths and hundredths) concretely, pictorially, and symbolically and round decimals to the nearest tenth
0 tenths and 7 hundredths make which decimal? The answer is 0.07. 0/10 plus 7/100 equals 0.07.
A ruler reading has 3 tenths and 8 hundredths of a metre. What decimal length is this? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 0.38. 3/10 plus 8/100 equals 0.38.

subject: mathematics
title: Adding and subtracting decimals
scenes: Learn to use models to explain the result of addition and subtraction of decimals (up to hundredths)
Calculate 0.40 plus 0.14. The answer is 0.54. Line up the decimal points and combine hundredths.
Kofi cuts 2.7 m from a 6.0 m rope. What length remains? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 3.3. Subtract: 6.0 minus 2.7 equals 3.3.

subject: mathematics
title: Percent out of 100 & Comparing fractions, decimals and percents
scenes: Learn to model or recognise percent (as a fraction related to hundredths) using concrete models, pictorial representations and number line and compare and order a mixture of common, decimal and percent fractions (up to hundredths)
Out of 100 equally sized squares, 88 are shaded. What percent is shaded? The answer is 88 percent. 88 out of 100 means 88 percent.
Out of 100 pupils, 40 prefer reading. What percentage is that? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 40 percent. 40 out of 100 means 40 percent.

subject: mathematics
title: Recognising number patterns & Finding missing terms
scenes: Learn to describe the pattern found in a given table or chart and determine the missing element(s) in a given table or chart
Which rule describes the pattern 17, 30, 43, ...? The answer is Add 13. Each next term increases by 13.
A walking counter records 16, 28, 40 steps. What is the change each time? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is plus 12. Each difference equals 12.

subject: mathematics
title: Finding pattern errors
scenes: Learn to identify the error(s) in a given table or chart
A table should add 5 each time: 25, 30, 36, 40. What should replace 36? The answer is 35. The correct third entry is 35.
A learner says 33, 40, 50, 54 goes up by 7. Which listed term is incorrect? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 50. The third step breaks the constant difference.

subject: mathematics
title: Making patterns with objects & Building tables from patterns
scenes: Learn to create a concrete representation of a given pattern displayed in a table or chart and create a table or chart from a given concrete representation of a pattern
A row has 4 dots, the next has 13, and the third has 22. How many in row four? The answer is 31. Add 9 dots each new row.
A line of bead rows grows from 34 to 39 to 44. How many beads should row five have? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 54. Add the fixed increase four times.

subject: mathematics
title: Turning stories into tables & Using tables to solve problems
scenes: Learn to translate information from a problem into a table or chart and identify and extend the patterns in a table or chart to solve a given problem
A village saves 7 cedis on Monday and increases savings by 16 cedis each day. What is Thursday’s saving? The answer is 55. Write a daily table and add the same step.
A reading club borrows 35 books on Monday, then 11 more each day. What is Thursday’s total? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 68. Thursday is three daily increases after Monday.

subject: mathematics
title: Equations from stories & Pictures and missing numbers
scenes: Learn to write a given problem as an equation in which a symbol is used to represent an unknown number and express a given pictorial or concrete representation of an equation in symbolic form
Kofi had some marbles. After receiving 33 more, he has 58. Which equation represents the unknown starting amount? The answer is n plus 33 equals 58. Let n be the marbles at the start.
Mansa had an unknown number of books; she receives 11 more and now owns 27. Which equation models her original books n? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is n plus 11 equals 27. The original plus added books equals the final total.

subject: mathematics
title: Model one-step equations & Explain unknowns
scenes: Learn to solve a given one-step equation using manipulatives and describe orally, the meaning of a given one-step equation with one unknown
Solve n plus 8 equals 33. The answer is 25. Undo addition: n equals 25.
If n plus 11 equals 36, how many counters represent n? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 25. 36 minus 11 equals 25.

subject: mathematics
title: Unknowns on either side & Guess and check
scenes: Learn to solve a given equation when the unknown is on the left or right side of the equation and solve a given one-step equation using “guess and check”
Solve n minus 16 equals 19. The answer is 35. Undo subtraction: n equals 35.
An unknown number minus 15 equals 13. Which guess is correct? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 28. 28 minus 15 equals 13.

subject: mathematics
title: Story equations & Part-part-whole equations
scenes: Learn to identify the unknown in a problem, represent the problem with an equation, and solve the problem concretely, pictorially or symbolically and represent and solve a given addition or subtraction problem involving a “part- part-whole” or comparison context, using a symbol to represent the unknown
30 pencils are in two boxes. One box has 8. Solve n plus 8 equals 30. The answer is 22. Subtract the known part from the whole.
Two friends have 33 balls altogether. One has 6. Write the missing amount. Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 27. 33 minus 6 equals 27.

subject: mathematics
title: Invent a word problem
scenes: Learn to create a problem for a given equation with one unknown
Which word problem fits n plus 8 equals 57? The answer is Start with n stickers, get 8 more, finish with 57. The plus sign shows an increase.
Which equation would solve “An unknown number of beads, plus 11 more, makes 18”? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is n plus 11 equals 18. The unknown beads plus the added beads gives the total.

subject: mathematics
title: Draw mirror images & Lines of symmetry
scenes: Learn to complete drawings of shapes to make them symmetrical and identify the lines of symmetry of regular and irregular 2d shapes (triangles and quadrilateral)
A point is 16 squares below a horizontal mirror line. Where must its reflection be drawn? The answer is 16 squares above. A reflection stays the same distance across the mirror line.
A dot is 8 squares left of a vertical mirror. Where should its reflected dot be? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 8 squares right. Reflection keeps the same distance across the mirror.

subject: mathematics
title: Compass directions
scenes: Learn to tell the position and motion of objects in space using the cardinal points north, south, east and west
A pupil walks 24 blocks east. Which compass direction is the pupil moving? The answer is east. Use a compass rose labelled N, S, E and W.
A learner walks toward north to school. To return on the same path, which direction must she walk? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is south. south is opposite north.

subject: mathematics
title: Estimating perimeter & Measuring perimeter
scenes: Learn to estimate perimeter using referents measured in centimetres or metres and measure and record perimeter for regular and irregular shapes in cm and m
Estimate the perimeter of a rectangle about 7 cm long and 12 cm wide using the side lengths. The answer is 38 cm. Add all four sides once: 2 times (length plus width).
A rectangular school garden measures 13 m by 3 m. How much fencing is needed for all four sides? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 32 m. 2 times (13 plus 3) equals 32 m.

subject: mathematics
title: Perimeter formulas & Same perimeter, different rectangles
scenes: Learn to develop and apply a formula for determining perimeter of square and rectangle and construct different rectangles for a given perimeter (cm, m) to demonstrate that many shapes are possible for a perimeter
Calculate the perimeter of a 7 m long, 10 m wide school garden. The answer is 34 m. P equals 2 times (7 plus 10) equals 34 m.
A rectangular school garden measures 15 m by 4 m. How much fencing is needed for all four sides? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 38 m. 2 times (15 plus 4) equals 38 m.

subject: mathematics
title: Understanding area & Choosing area units
scenes: Learn to recognise that area is measured in square units and select and justify referents for the units cm2 or m2
A floor is covered by 5 rows of 12 equal square tiles. How many square units of area does it cover? The answer is 60. Area means count all 60 unit squares.
A display mat has 14 rows with 3 square tiles each. How many square units are covered? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 42. 14 times 3 equals 42.

subject: mathematics
title: Estimating area & Area formulas
scenes: Learn to estimate area by using referents for cm2 or m2 and develop and apply a formula for determining area of a rectangle and square
Estimate the number of 1 cm squared tiles covering a 10 cm by 7 cm rectangle. The answer is 70. Each unit square contributes 1 cm squared .
A display mat has 9 rows with 2 square tiles each. How many square units are covered? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 18. 9 times 2 equals 18.

subject: mathematics
title: Same area, different rectangles
scenes: Learn to construct different rectangles for a given area (cm2 or m2) in order to demonstrate that many different rectangles may have the same area
A rectangle has area 10 cm squared and length 2 cm. What is the width? The answer is 5 cm. 10 divided by 2 equals 5.
A rectangular plot is 3 m by 3 m. What total area does the plot cover? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 9 m squared total. 3 times 3 equals 9.

subject: mathematics
title: Clock times & Timing events
scenes: Learn to tell the time in hours and minutes in analogue and digital watches including 24-hour clocks and use clock to measure time to complete simple events in minutes and seconds
Write 12:00 in 24-hour time if it is in the afternoon. The answer is 12:00. For PM hours 1–11, add 12 to the hour.
A lesson begins at 2:15 PM. What time is that on a 24-hour clock? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 14:15. Add 12 to the PM hour for 1–11 PM.

subject: mathematics
title: Writing calendar dates
scenes: Learn to state dates of events and record calendar dates in a variety of formats
Write 24 December 2026 as DD/MM/YYYY. The answer is 24/12/2026. Day first, then month, then four-digit year.
A school fair is on 13/03/2028. What is the date 1 day later? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 14/03/2028. Advance the calendar by one day.

subject: mathematics
title: One symbol, one item & Pictograph keys
scenes: Learn to use an understanding of one-to-one correspondence to read and interpret graphs and use an understanding of many-to-one correspondence to display or construct graphs
In a chart, one picture means one pupil. There are 7 orange pictures. How many pupils chose orange? The answer is 7. One symbol represents one pupil.
A pictograph uses one picture for one pupil. There are 17 pictures of mangoes. How many pupils chose them? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 17. Each symbol represents one pupil.

subject: mathematics
title: Comparing charts & Graphs in everyday life
scenes: Learn to compare graphs in which the same data has been displayed and explain how they are the same and different and find examples of graphs in which many-to-one correspondence is used in print and electronic media, such as newspapers, magazines and the internet, and describe the correspondence used
A table lists orange: 26 and banana: 8. How many more are in the larger group? The answer is 18. Subtract the smaller bar height from the larger.
A bar chart shows mangoes: 24 and bananas: 11. What is the difference between their bars? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 13. Subtract the smaller count.

subject: mathematics
title: Create a graph & Read graphs to decide
scenes: Learn to identify common features of graphs that use many-to-one correspondence and use that understanding to draw bar graphs or pictographs, complete with title, labelled axes, key or legend, to represent data collected (up to 4 categories of data) and use understanding of many-to-one correspondence to solve simple problems (how many altogether, comparing, or take apart problems) requiring interpretation of many-to- one bar graphs (up to 4 categories of data)
A bar chart displays banana equals 36. Which bar height should be used? The answer is 36. The labelled vertical axis must reach the recorded value.
A class recorded 4 votes for mangoes. How high should its bar be on an axis marked in ones? Pause and solve it in your exercise book.
The answer is 4. Bar height equals the recorded total.

subject: english
title: Explaining Messages and Values in Songs
scenes: Songs can communicate community values and central messages. Give evidence from lyrics and connect the message with everyday choices.
A singer makes the important word louder. Which feature is used? Answer: Stress
Explain the central message of a song and describe a real situation that illustrates its value.
Why it works: Stress draws attention to a meaningful word.

subject: english
title: Responding to and Composing Six-Line Poems
scenes: A six-line poem uses a connected idea, vivid words, fitting rhythm and purposeful sound patterns. A thoughtful response explains its central theme.
Why does a poet choose an image such as “silver moon”? Answer: It helps a reader picture the scene.
Compose six original lines about a Ghanaian place and explain the value expressed by your poem.
Why it works: An image makes an idea vivid.

subject: english
title: Stories: Moral Lessons and Parallel Narratives
scenes: A story connects character choices and consequences. A parallel story uses a comparable lesson in a fresh setting without copying the original plot.
Why is a story's setting useful? Answer: It tells where or when events happen.
Retell a folktale's lesson, then invent a different story showing the same moral.
Why it works: Setting places events in a context.

subject: english
title: Dramatising Stories with Costume and Gesture
scenes: Dramatisation uses costume, gesture, dialogue, expression and purposeful movement to show character and meaning.
Why is a story's setting useful? Answer: It tells where or when events happen.
Perform a two-minute sketch based on a reading story; select a safe costume to help show character.
Why it works: Setting places events in a context.

subject: english
title: Judging Characters and Building a Sketch
scenes: Interpret moral values using what characters say, do and cause; adapt a short narrative into a clear scene with a beginning and ending.
Which detail belongs in a short retelling? Answer: The central problem and how it was solved.
Create a sketch about honesty or kindness, perform it and discuss a character's decision.
Why it works: Important events help the retelling make sense.

subject: english
title: Describing Ghanaian Regions and Places
scenes: An effective oral description names a real Ghanaian place and accurately explains its location, notable features and cultural significance.
Which question helps describe an event fully? Answer: Who took part and what did they do?
Present a short factual talk about one of Ghana's regions, identifying a place and a distinctive feature.
Why it works: Who and what identify participants and action.

subject: english
title: Attentive Listening, Posture and Expression
scenes: Listening includes sustained attention, suitable posture, relevant facial expression, brief notes and accurate recall of what was heard.
“An old tree shaded the school playground.” Which detail shows a benefit? Answer: It shaded the playground.
Listen to a classmate's announcement without interruption; report its topic and two key details.
Why it works: Shade is a benefit for learners.

subject: english
title: Collaborative Conversation and Clarification
scenes: Conversation requires fair turns, relevant questions, clarification requests and respectful responses to others' points.
Which greeting suits a visitor in the afternoon? Answer: Good afternoon; welcome.
Discuss making your school greener. Ask one clarifying question and give a reasoned reply.
Why it works: The greeting matches the time and occasion.

subject: english
title: Think-Aloud, Inferences and Cause-and-Effect — Part 1
scenes: Think aloud while listening or reading: connect prior knowledge, recognise cause and effect, use evidence and draw a sensible conclusion.
“An old tree shaded the school playground.” Which detail shows a benefit? Answer: It shaded the playground.
Tell a short story, identify an event's cause and effect, and explain the conclusion supported by its details.
Why it works: Shade is a benefit for learners.

subject: english
title: Think-Aloud, Inferences and Cause-and-Effect — Part 2
scenes: Think aloud while listening or reading: connect prior knowledge, recognise cause and effect, use evidence and draw a sensible conclusion.
“Ama sorted paper and plastic into separate bins.” What is the main idea? Answer: Ama separated waste for recycling.
Tell a short story, identify an event's cause and effect, and explain the conclusion supported by its details.
Why it works: The central action is sorting waste.

subject: english
title: Using Do, Be and Have as Helping Verbs
scenes: Auxiliary verbs do, be and have help form questions, negatives and verb phrases. Match each auxiliary to the subject and tense.
Which sentence correctly uses do as a helping verb? Answer: Do they play after school?
Say or write three questions using do/does, is/are and has/have correctly.
The plural subject they takes do and a base verb.

subject: english
title: Question Tags and Auxiliary Responses
scenes: A confirmation tag usually changes positive to negative or negative to positive and uses the appropriate helping verb.
Complete: “They aren't late, blank ?” Answer: are they
Practise ten tag questions aloud with a partner, checking tense and positive/negative balance.
Why it works: A negative 'are not' statement takes 'are they?'.

subject: english
title: Giving Instructions and Making Polite Requests
scenes: Clear instructions use action verbs and logical steps. Polite requests include respectful words and a realistic response.
Which greeting suits a visitor in the afternoon? Answer: Good afternoon; welcome.
Tell a partner how to prepare a reading notebook and ask for help politely.
Why it works: The greeting matches the time and occasion.

subject: english
title: Meaning through Voice, Pace and Gesture
scenes: Volume, pace, pitch, emphasis, gesture and facial expression change how an audience understands spoken words.
What is the purpose of a full stop during oral reading? Answer: Pause and mark the end of a sentence.
Say a sentence as a warning and as an invitation; compare tone and expression.
Why it works: Pausing marks the sentence ending.

subject: english
title: Audible Speaking and Expressive Reading
scenes: Fluent spoken reading is clear, appropriately paced, accurate and expressive; self-correction supports understanding.
What is the purpose of a full stop during oral reading? Answer: Pause and mark the end of a sentence.
Read a passage twice and record where your pacing, expression or pronunciation improved.
Why it works: Pausing marks the sentence ending.

subject: english
title: Planning and Delivering a Supported Speech — Part 1
scenes: Plan a speech around a purpose and audience; gather facts, arrange arguments, use examples and clear signposts, and speak confidently.
Which audience suits a school notice? Answer: Learners and school staff.
Deliver a two-minute speech on water safety with an introduction, three points, evidence and a conclusion.
Why it works: Notices give information to the school community.

subject: english
title: Planning and Delivering a Supported Speech — Part 2
scenes: Plan a speech around a purpose and audience; gather facts, arrange arguments, use examples and clear signposts, and speak confidently.
Why make a plan before writing? Answer: To organise ideas logically.
Deliver a two-minute speech on water safety with an introduction, three points, evidence and a conclusion.
Why it works: Planning guides the draft.

subject: english
title: Hard and Soft Consonants and r-Controlled Words
scenes: The pronunciation of letters can depend on neighbouring letters. In words like car and bird, r changes the vowel sound; suffixes alter syllable patterns.
Which word contains the sound /th/ as in thin? Answer: thumb
Sort words by hard/soft c and g sounds, then read r-controlled words and words with suffixes.
Why it works: Thumb begins with th.

subject: english
title: Minimal Pairs and Digraph Words
scenes: A minimal pair differs by one speech sound, such as ship/sheep; distinguishing that sound helps decoding and clear meaning.
Which words differ by just one vowel sound? Answer: ship and sheep
Sort minimal pairs by changed sound, then use new digraph words in original sentences.
Ship /ɪ/ and sheep /iː/ differ in a vowel.

subject: english
title: Closing Diphthongs in Words
scenes: A closing diphthong moves the tongue toward a second vowel position, as in the /aʊ/ of now and /əʊ/ of go (in many accents).
Which word has the closing diphthong /aʊ/ (as in now)? Answer: cow
Read several examples of the closing diphthongs in now and go, paying attention to pronunciation.
Cow shares the gliding vowel in now.

subject: english
title: Blending Two-Syllable Words
scenes: Blend sounds into syllables, then join syllables to read a longer word. Check the word's meaning and conventional spelling.
Which word begins with the digraph sh? Answer: ship
Break six two-syllable words into their component syllables and blend them again.
Why it works: The letters sh represent a single consonant sound.

subject: english
title: Synonyms, Antonyms and Word Parts
scenes: Precise vocabulary includes synonyms, antonyms, useful affixes and content-specific word meanings.
Which word means a place where books are borrowed? Answer: library
Collect five terms from Science and write a synonym or antonym where one exists.
Why it works: Libraries lend reading materials.

subject: english
title: Vocabulary Growth Through Extensive Reading
scenes: Reading varied genres builds vocabulary. Guess meanings from context, verify, and use new words in original sentences.
Which word best describes someone who helps others? Answer: helpful
Keep a reading vocabulary journal with at least five words and sentences.
Why it works: Helpful means ready to assist.

subject: english
title: Meaning from Word Class and Context
scenes: A word's grammatical role, surrounding clues and relationships with other words can help determine its meaning.
“Ama was relieved when she found her missing key.” Relieved means what? Answer: No longer worried
Use context to explain a noun, a verb and an adjective from an unfamiliar reading passage.
Why it works: Finding the key removes worry.

subject: english
title: Acronyms, Wordplay and Audience
scenes: Acronyms use initial letters of words; playful language depends on audience and context. Use formal language where precision is important.
What do the letters in an acronym usually stand for? Answer: Parts of a longer name or phrase
Create an original acronym for a school group and explain it; rewrite an informal message formally.
Acronyms are built from initial letters of words.

subject: english
title: Main Ideas, Skimming and Scanning
scenes: Skim to find the gist; scan for a precise fact; read closely to connect main ideas and supporting details in order.
“Abena returned a lost purse to its owner.” Which value does the action show? Answer: Honesty
Read a short nonfiction text, identify its main idea, scan for two facts and justify your answer.
Why it works: Returning property shows honesty.

subject: english
title: Critical Reading and Comparing Ideas
scenes: Reasoned judgments about a text need evidence, not guesses. Compare related claims and decide what each supports.
“Ama sorted paper and plastic into separate bins.” What is the main idea? Answer: Ama separated waste for recycling.
Read two short paragraphs and identify one point of agreement and one difference using text evidence.
Why it works: The central action is sorting waste.

subject: english
title: Text Structure and Word Analysis
scenes: Identify introductions, bodies and conclusions. Prefixes and suffixes can support decoding and changing meanings.
Which word contains a prefix meaning wrongly? Answer: misread
Mark the three parts of an informational text and explain two words with affixes.
Why it works: Mis- can mean wrongly.

subject: english
title: Inferences and Contextual Meaning
scenes: An inference goes beyond what a passage says directly but must still be supported by its details.
“Abena returned a lost purse to its owner.” Which value does the action show? Answer: Honesty
Read a short passage and answer literal, vocabulary and inference questions with supporting clues.
Why it works: Returning property shows honesty.

subject: english
title: Fluency and Self-Correction in Reading
scenes: Read accurately, with natural phrasing and a suitable pace; notice when words do not fit the context and correct them.
A learner rushes and misses small words. What should improve? Answer: Slow to a manageable pace and check accuracy.
Read aloud for one minute and reread a paragraph more accurately after feedback.
Why it works: Accurate pace supports comprehension.

subject: english
title: Oral and Written Summaries
scenes: Summaries retain the central point and essential supporting events, not every minor detail or repeated phrase.
What comes first when preparing a summary? Answer: Read the whole text for its central idea.
Summarise a text orally, then write a five-sentence version in your own words.
Why it works: The gist guides selection.

subject: english
title: Count, Non-Count and Collective Nouns
scenes: Count nouns can be counted, while non-count nouns usually take measures; collective nouns name groups.
Which word usually names something we cannot count as separate items without a measure? Answer: water
Sort rice, chairs, team and water, then write appropriate quantity expressions.
Water is commonly a non-count noun.

subject: english
title: Articles and Determiners in Context — Part 1
scenes: Use a or an for singular unspecified count nouns and the for specific nouns. Other determiners express number, choice and reference.
Complete “Please pass me blank book on the desk.” Answer: the
Edit a paragraph using a, an, the, each, many, some and these appropriately.
Why it works: The identifies a specific book.

subject: english
title: Articles and Determiners in Context — Part 2
scenes: Use a or an for singular unspecified count nouns and the for specific nouns. Other determiners express number, choice and reference.
Which article completes “ blank orange”? Answer: an
Edit a paragraph using a, an, the, each, many, some and these appropriately.
Why it works: Use an before a vowel sound.

subject: english
title: Indefinite Pronouns in Sentences
scenes: Indefinite pronouns such as someone, anybody, everyone and nothing refer without naming a precise person or thing.
Which word is an indefinite pronoun? Answer: someone
Write five meaningful sentences using different indefinite pronouns.
Someone refers to an unspecified person.

subject: english
title: Regular and Irregular Comparisons
scenes: Use -er/-est or more/most as suitable; irregular comparisons include good, better, best.
What is the comparative of good? Answer: better
Describe and compare three items using regular and irregular adjective forms.
Why it works: Better is an irregular comparative.

subject: english
title: Present and Past Verb Forms and Agreement — Part 1
scenes: Use correct simple, continuous and perfect verb forms; agree with the subject and keep tense consistent.
Complete “The children blank football at break.” Answer: play
Revise a paragraph containing present, past and perfect tense errors; explain your changes.
Why it works: Plural children takes play.

subject: english
title: Present and Past Verb Forms and Agreement — Part 2
scenes: Use correct simple, continuous and perfect verb forms; agree with the subject and keep tense consistent.
Which is a verb in “Kofi carried a basket”? Answer: carried
Revise a paragraph containing present, past and perfect tense errors; explain your changes.
Why it works: Carried shows an action.

subject: english
title: Adverbs Showing How Actions Happen
scenes: Adverbs of manner tell how something occurs, as in carefully, politely or quickly; choose the form that matches meaning.
Complete the report: “The scientist recorded the results blank .” Choose an adverb that tells how. Answer: carefully
Describe how five classroom actions happen using different adverbs of manner.
Carefully is an adverb of manner; it describes how the action happens.

subject: english
title: Idioms and Their Real Meanings
scenes: Idioms express a meaning that is not always the sum of literal words; context reveals intended use.
Someone says “hit the books”. What do they intend? Answer: Study seriously.
Explain five common idioms in different real-life scenarios.
Why it works: The idiom means study.

subject: english
title: Conjunctions Expressing Reasons and Conditions
scenes: Because, since, although and unless connect clauses and clarify cause, contrast or conditions.
Complete “Ama blank Kofi read together.” Answer: and
Join sentences with conjunctions that correctly express reason, contrast and condition.
Why it works: And connects two people doing an activity.

subject: english
title: Modals for Ability, Permission and Obligation
scenes: Use can, could, may, might, must, should and would to show ability, likelihood, duty or advice.
Which sentence expresses possibility? Answer: It might rain later.
Explain changes in meaning when must is replaced with might in safety rules.
Why it works: Might signals possibility.

subject: english
title: Prepositions Across Time and Place
scenes: Prepositions show relations including position, movement, time and purpose; select them by meaning.
Which shows comparison? “Yaw is taller blank Kofi.” Answer: than
Describe the route to a library and its opening times using appropriate prepositions.
Why it works: Than introduces comparison.

subject: english
title: Joining Letters Neatly in Handwriting
scenes: Joined handwriting should be legible, appropriately spaced and consistent, with clear complete sentences.
What is the subject of “The pupils planted maize”? Answer: The pupils
Copy six full sentences in neat joined script and self-check spacing and punctuation.
Why it works: The subject names who performed the action.

subject: english
title: Selecting a Writing Mode for Your Audience
scenes: A writing task needs a clear purpose, intended reader, and appropriate format: letter, report, story or explanation.
Which sentence is a topic sentence? Answer: Our school garden needs regular care.
Convert the same school message into a friendly note and a short formal notice.
Why it works: A topic sentence introduces the paragraph's main point.

subject: english
title: Choosing and Narrowing a Writing Topic
scenes: Choose one clear topic, gather reliable details and avoid irrelevant points.
Which sentence is a topic sentence? Answer: Our school garden needs regular care.
Plan a focused two-paragraph text about protecting drinking water.
Why it works: A topic sentence introduces the paragraph's main point.

subject: english
title: Developing a Connected Two-Paragraph Draft
scenes: Organise related details around two clear main ideas with a logical link between paragraphs.
Which sentence is a topic sentence? Answer: Our school garden needs regular care.
Write two connected paragraphs about a school improvement with supporting details.
Why it works: A topic sentence introduces the paragraph's main point.

subject: english
title: Revising Ideas and Proofreading Writing
scenes: Revision improves content, paragraph organisation and clarity; proofreading corrects grammar, punctuation and spelling.
Which revision removes repetition? Answer: The pupils planted trees and watered them.
Exchange two paragraphs with a partner, revise their ideas and proofread the final version.
Why it works: Concise wording avoids unnecessary repetition.

subject: english
title: Settings, Characters and Plots in Narratives
scenes: A narrative needs an identifiable setting, believable characters, a problem, ordered events and a resolution.
A child returned extra change to a trader. Which value did the child show? Answer: Honesty
Create an original story with two characters, a setting, a challenge and a convincing ending.
Why it works: Returning what is not yours is honest.

subject: english
title: Creative Writing About Daily Life
scenes: Creative writing develops original situations, feelings, dialogue and imagery into coherent writing.
Which pair of words rhymes? Answer: light and night
Write a vivid short account about a school festival with realistic details.
Why it works: Light and night share a final sound.

subject: english
title: Using Sensory Details in Description
scenes: Choose precise sensory details and a clear order so a reader can picture a person, place or event.
When reporting a school event, which detail gives time? Answer: Friday morning at nine.
Describe a Ghanaian market in a paragraph using sound, colour and movement.
Why it works: A stated time locates the event.

subject: english
title: Explaining Opinions with Clear Reasons
scenes: An opinion becomes more convincing when explained with relevant reasons and examples.
What is a respectful way to disagree? Answer: I understand your view, but here is another reason.
Write a reasoned paragraph about daily reading at home.
Why it works: Reasoned disagreement stays respectful.

subject: english
title: Claims, Evidence and Persuasive Writing
scenes: Introduce a claim, support it with reasons and credible examples, and close with a purposeful conclusion.
What does evidence do in persuasive writing? Answer: Supports a claim with facts or examples.
Write two paragraphs persuading your school to protect a reading area, citing real examples.
Why it works: Evidence strengthens a claim.

subject: english
title: Explaining a Process Step by Step
scenes: Process explanations use clear time-order phrases, imperative or present-tense verbs and complete steps.
Which word shows the first stage in instructions? Answer: First
Write instructions for washing hands, describing why the order matters.
First introduces the opening step.

subject: english
title: Reporting an Event Clearly
scenes: Report events in chronological order using specific who, what, when, where and what-happened details.
Esi watered a dry seedling; days later new leaves appeared. What caused the change? Answer: Regular watering and care.
Write two paragraphs about a school event with facts arranged chronologically.
Why it works: Care helped the plant grow.

subject: english
title: Writing a Personal Letter About an Event
scenes: A friendly letter uses an address/date, greeting, coherent body, appropriate closing and correct audience tone.
Where does a date usually appear in a traditional friendly letter? Answer: Near the beginning, before the greeting.

title: Comparing experimental and theoretical probability
scenes: Observed frequency divided by number of trials is experimental probability; it approaches theory with more trials.

Write the observed heads frequency as a fraction: 59 heads in 120 trials. The answer is 59/120. Experimental probability equals observed heads divided by total tosses equals 59/120; it may differ from 1/2.
